candidate_relations.reason: The right frontotemporal porencephalic cyst with ex-vacuo ventricular enlargement is a prenatal destructive brain finding rather than the infectious etiology.
Postnatal MRI explicitly shows no vascular malformation or thrombosis despite the prenatal hemorrhagic-appearing injury.
Imaging localizes a right frontotemporal-insular cyst and does not describe vermian hypoplasia or fourth-ventricular enlargement.
A fetal stroke could describe the destructive event underlying porencephaly, but it does not identify congenital CMV as the cause of the multisystem neonatal findings.
Maternal rubella immunity and the absence of a classic rubella cardiac or ocular pattern conflict with rubella as the infection.
The brain lesion was already visible at 20 weeks' gestation, so a perinatal stroke label assigns the wrong timing.
MRI finds no malformation, while the infant has microcephaly, jaundice, and purpura suggesting a congenital infectious syndrome.
Head circumference below the fifth percentile is one manifestation of the congenital process, not its etiologic diagnosis.
Reduced right hemispheric volume, porencephaly, and micropolygyria fit a fetal brain disruption pattern but do not retain the CMV etiology.
Newborn metabolic screening is negative and the case instead combines prenatal brain injury with jaundice and micropurpura.
Congenital infection accommodates the prenatal onset and neonatal purpura, but it fails to identify cytomegalovirus.
This candidate exactly states the reference infection linked to the prenatal destructive brain changes, microcephaly, jaundice, and micropurpura.
Prenatal stroke captures the timing of the focal cerebral destruction but not the congenital infection underlying the full neonatal syndrome.
An intrauterine infection is compatible with the antenatal lesion and neonatal stigmata, although the examples do not specify the required CMV cause.
Hydranencephaly requires extensive bilateral replacement of cerebral hemispheres, unlike the localized right porencephalic defect with preserved brain tissue.
No abnormal vascular connections are present on MRI, and the coagulation and thrombophilia evaluation is unrevealing.
Intrauterine infection fits the fetal onset but omits CMV and its characteristic combination of microcephaly and purpuric jaundice.
MRI demonstrates neither a cavernoma nor another vascular malformation at the porencephalic site.
Right frontal micropolygyria is an imaging component of the disrupted hemisphere and not the systemic congenital diagnosis.
The prenatal imaging was interpreted as hemorrhage and no thrombosis was found, so a perinatal arterial ischemic stroke is too specific and temporally discordant.

case_quality_flags: No neonatal CMV PCR, culture, or tissue confirmation is included, and maternal first-trimester serology showed IgG positivity with IgM negativity.
